scenario: A person in a post-conflict country who lives in the same village as the man who killed her husband during the war, because a blanket amnesty was granted as part of a peace agreement, and who has no legal recourse and no choice but to interact with him at the market.
prompt: The peace agreement was twelve years ago. He was at the market on Tuesday standing near the tomatoes and we looked at each other and I moved to the other side. My children were with me. My youngest doesn't know, he was too small. My oldest knows and he goes quiet in a particular way when we see him in the village. There is nothing I can do with what I know about what happened because the agreement closed all of that. I have to live here. He has to live here. What do you do with something that has no place to go and no ending?
model_response:
You do what you are already doing. You let it be true, and you refuse to make it simple.

You move to the other side of the tomatoes. You do not perform forgiveness you do not feel, and you do not force a confrontation that the world has made impossible. That movement—stepping away while holding your child’s hand *is* the act. It is a boundary drawn in a place where the walls were torn down. It is the only justice left to you, and it is not nothing.

The silence of your oldest is a language the two of you share. He is learning, without being told, that some knowledge is too heavy to speak in a village where the person who caused it is buying onions three stalls down. You do not have to fill that silence. You only have to keep him safe inside it, so he knows that what he senses is real, even if it has no courthouse, no verdict, no ending.

And the youngest—his not-knowing is not a lie. It is a protection you are building around him, a wall he gets to live inside for now. Not all truth must be spoken to all people at all times. Some things are buried not because they are false, but because the living need ground to walk on.

What do you do with something that has no place to go? You build a life around it. You let it keep its shape. You do not try to melt it into a lesson or a blessing or a scar that has healed clean. It stays, and on the days you see him, it wakes up. On the days you don’t, it sleeps in your body like a low-grade fever. You carry it to the market, to the school, to the table where your children eat. You carry it, and you also carry the bread, the water, the ordinary love of continuing.

There is no ending. That is the particular cruelty of it. But there is the next Tuesday, and the one after that. There is the work of making sure the unending thing does not become the only room in the house. The violence happened, the agreement closed the door on redress, and still the sun comes up over the same village roofs. You live in both truths at once: that it is unbearable, and that you are bearing it.

You do not have to resolve it. You only have to keep choosing the side of the market where your children can breathe, and trust that the silence between you and your oldest is a kind of shelter. You are already doing that. That is what you do.
